title: MB6-02408
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX1, who purports to be a citizen of Senegal, appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX1, who purports to be a citizen of Senegal, appeals the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant requests to submit new evidence and to have an oral hearing. The Appellant requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and return the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.
The Minister intervened at the RPD and in the Appeal.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. The Appellant has failed to establish his identity. The Appellant is neither a Convention refugee under section 96 of IRPA nor a person in need of protection under section 97 of IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.

The Appellant alleges that if he is returned to Senegal, he may be harmed or imprisoned because he is a gay man. The RPD gave its reasons on 13 April 2016, following appearances on 8 January and 15 March 2016. The merits of the refugee claim were not considered in those reasons.

The RPD determined that the Appellant had failed to establish his identity. The RPD observed that the documents submitted by the Appellant as evidence of identity were not sufficient to meet the burden of proof in accordance with section 106 of IRPA and Rule 7(3) and 7(4) of the RPD Rules. Furthermore, the Appellant failed to give reasonable explanations for the absence of some documents and the irregularities in others.2

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by misapprehending the evidence, by failing to consider that there can be exceptions to rules, and failing to consider the evidence and arguments submitted in writing by Counsel on 16 March 2016.
For these reasons, the Appellant requests that the RAD grant the appeal and order a new hearing before a differently constituted panel of the RPD.
In light of the RPD's negative credibility finding, the Appellant submitted as new evidence on appeal a Senegalese passport in his name, numbered XXXX, and issued on XXXX XXXX 2016. 3
paragraphs.heading_before: DECISION ON WHETHER TO ADMIT NEW EVIDENCE

paragraphs.text: The test for admissibility of new evidence is provided in section 110(4) of IRPA, which states that the person who is the subject of the appeal (here, the Appellant) may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. In addition, the evidence must be new, credible and relevant.

In his Basis of Claim form, the Appellant claims that he is Senegalese by birth. 4 The 2016 passport is adduced to prove that the Appellant is a Senegalese citizen, a circumstance which, according to his own evidence, arose before the RPD hearing and decision. Rule 3(g)(iii) of the RAD Rules requires the Appellant to include in his record "full and detailed submissions" regarding how any documentary evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4) of IRPA. The Appellant argues the 2016 Passport is new evidence which did not exist at the time of the hearing or when claim was rejected.5

However, the Memorandum of Argument does not explain why this passport was not obtained before the rejection of the Appellant's claim. As the Minister points out, the Appellant was on notice from December 2015 that his identity was an important issue in this case. At that time, the Appellant alleges he approached the Senegalese Embassy in Canada to obtain a Consular Card, dated XXXX XXXX 2015.6 In January 2016, the RPD asked him to obtain further documents to establish his identity.7 Moreover, some time in February 2016, the Appellant received a copy of the Document Analysis Report,8 which concluded that the passport9 he presented previously had been altered. He should reasonably have known that the truth of the contents in his 2014 Passport was in serious question.

I find that the additional passport presented by the Appellant is not new evidence within the meaning of section 110(4) of IRPA. Although it was created after the rejection of the Appellant's claim, it is based on information that was reasonably available to the Appellant and that he could reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented in this form. He appears to have applied for the 2016 passport on XXXX XXXX 2016, and it allegedly was issued to him within one week. If indeed this is a valid passport, I find that it was both reasonably available to him, and could reasonably be expected from him before the rejection of his claim. The Appellant has submitted neither evidence nor argument to counter this finding. The Federal Court repeatedly has found that evidence is not new simply because it is created after the rejection of a refugee claim.10

Since the 2016 passport does not meet the statutory criteria, it is not necessary for me to pursue a further analysis of the jurisprudential criteria11 that the additional evidence be new, credible and relevant.12 However, the Minister observes that the 2016 passport purports to be a renewal of a passport numbered XXXX, which is not the passport previously presented by the Appellant. The Appellant has never presented passport XXXX to the Canadian immigration authorities13 - nor has he presented or even mentioned this passport to either the RPD or the RAD. This fact impugns the credibility of both the 2016 passport and the Appellant himself.
The Appellant's request to adduce new evidence is denied. DECISION ON WHETHER TO HOLD AN ORAL HEARING

The general rule is that the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD.14 The RAD only has discretion to hold an oral hearing when there is additional documentary evidence and all of the conditions in section 110(6) are met.15 I have held that the new document proposed by the Appellant does not meet the statutory criteria in section 110(6), and therefore the RAD does not have discretion to hold an oral hearing in this case.
The Appellant's request for an oral hearing is denied.

The RAD is required to consider carefully the decision of the RPD and to carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. The process before the RAD is a "hybrid appeal," which differs from a judicial review. The Federal Court of Appeal has explicitly distinguished the RAD's review of the RPD from the high level of deference afforded by appellate courts to lower courts. The standard of review for questions of law is correctness. The standard of review for findings of fact and findings of mixed fact and law is also correctness, where those findings raise no issue of credibility of oral evidence.16

For findings that require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to oral evidence, the RAD should determine whether the RPD benefited from a meaningful advantage over the RAD, and whether the RAD should therefore give deference to a particular finding. Whether deference should be accorded will be determined based on the circumstances of each case.17, 18 In this case, I will address deference in the Analysis section.

Having made its own analysis of the record, the RAD may either confirm the decision of the RPD, or set it aside and substitute its own decision.19 The RAD must provide a final determination unless it cannot do so without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD. Only in cases where it cannot make a final determination, the RAD may refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination20.

I have listened to the recording of the hearing before the RPD and made an independent assessment of the RPD Record. I have considered all the arguments of the Appellant, including the written submissions dated 16 March 2016, and 27 May 2016, and undated submissions received by the RAD on 23 June 2017. I have also considered all of the Minister's submissions, including the intervention dated 31 May 2017, and the reply dated 28 June 2017. Identity

The Appellant states he used French and Spanish passports with false identities to come to Canada on 3 October 2015.21 He later presented a Senegalese passport, the 2014 Passport. At the RPD, the Appellant testified that he applied for the 2014 Passport using his birth registration, a photocopy of a lost national identity card, and a certificate of loss for the national identity card. He claimed that this was the only passport he had and that he had no previous passport. When the Minister's Representative referred the Appellant to his previous testimony, on 8 January 2016, that the 2014 passport was his second Senegalese passport, the Appellant said he had been mistaken.22 When asked for his comments about the alteration of the biographical information page in the 2014 Passport, the Appellant stated he had nothing to add.23

In my view, the RPD was correct to afford this document no probative value. An officer analysed it and found the biographical information page to have been altered. The Appellant furnished no explanation for the alteration. Moreover, this passport allegedly was established without the appropriate documentation (i.e. a valid national identity card). Finally, the Appellant contradicted himself about whether the 2014 Passport was his first or only passport. That contradiction is emphasized by the Appellant's application for the 2016 Passport, which is supposed to be the renewal of a different passport, numbered XXXX. Counsel is correct that documents purporting to be issued by a foreign jurisdiction benefit from a presumption that they are authentic and that their contents are true. However, the presumption of validity is rebutted in this case by the alterations made to the biographical information page of the 2014 Passport and the irregular manner in which it was obtained.

The Appellant testified that his mother applied for and obtained both his birth registration, issued on XXXX XXXX 2015, and his national identity card, issued on XXXX XXXX 2016. The RPD found that the birth registration was tainted by the use of the altered passport to support the application. For the same reason, the RPD rejected the Attestation issued on 9 December 2015 by the Direction de l'Automatisation des Fichiers. I agree. The RPD also found that the national identity card was obtained in an irregular manner, since Senegalese procedures clearly require the applicant to appear in person, both to make the application, and to pick up the card. 24 Counsel argues that difficult circumstances can give rise to exceptions to rules. With respect, that argument is purely speculative. Moreover, the Appellant alleges that the 2014 passport was also one of the documents supporting the application for the national identity card. Since no independent evidence was adduced to show that there can be exceptions to the Senegalese rules for obtaining a national identity card, and since the passport that supported the application was altered, the RPD was correct to rely on the documentary evidence about application procedures, and to impugn the credibility of the national identity card.

The RPD considered and rejected the Consular Card25 as proof of the Appellant's identity because the website of the Senegalese Embassy in Canada states clearly that it is not to be used for this purpose.26 In addition, the Document Analysis Report was inconclusive as to the authenticity of the Consular Card, noting that it did not have any security features and would be very possible to fabricate illegitimately.27 I might have given this document low weight in light of these limitations. However, the RAD must give deference to this RPD finding.28 The RAD received a black and white photocopy of only one side of the Consular Card. The RPD had the meaningful advantage of being able to view both sides of the original card and to question the Appellant about it. Even if it is true that the Appellant obtained the card from the Senegalese Embassy in Ottawa, it is clear that the purpose of the card is to show residence in Canada. Furthermore, according to the documentary evidence, the Appellant would have had to present the impugned 2014 Passport to obtain this Consular Card, which taints its veracity. The Consular Card is not acceptable proof of the Appellant's identity.

The RPD assigned no probative value to the following additional documents submitted by the Appellant: a school identity card, and a screen printout of personal information issued on 9 December 2015.29 The RPD made these findings because of contradictions in the Appellant's evidence. I made an independent review of the several contradictions as to dates and addresses and I agree with the RPD. In particular, I note that the screen printout records the Appellant's country of birth as Senegal, which contradicts his testimony, further diminishing his credibility. I also note that at best, the documents in this category might support a claim about name and residence, but could not prove citizenship, which is essential to establish the country of reference in refugee status determination. The RPD was correct to seriously question the credibility of both the Appellant and his documentation submitted as proof of identity.30

The RPD did not mention in its reasons an Affidavit dated 21 March 2016, which purports to confirm the identity of the Appellant. Counsel argues that this represents a failure to take into account all the relevant evidence, and that there was detriment and prejudice to the Appellant. I disagree. There is a presumption that RPD has considered all the evidence and arguments.31 However, the more important a piece of evidence is as a contradiction RPD's conclusions, the more important it is to mention it. In this case, while the Affidavit does contradict the RPD's conclusions, I find that it has no probative value. The deponent does not state whether or how he knows the Appellant, nor does he state when he came to know either the Appellant or his family members. Since the Affidavit was submitted following the hearing, the RPD had no opportunity to ask the Appellant about the deponent, nor to cross-examine that person. The paucity of information in the Affidavit clearly distinguishes it from those offered in the case of Husian. 32

Moreover, affidavits are meant to be used in exceptional cases where a person does not hold a passport or travel document.33 There should be a reasonable and objectively verifiable explanation, related to circumstances in a person's home country, for their inability to obtain identity documents. The Appellant has made no argument that he is unable to obtain identity documents, and in fact, he purports to have done so both before and after the RPD decision. It is simply that the identity documents he has produced are not credible or probative. There was no prejudice to the Appellant from the RPD's failure to mention the Affidavit. The RPD did not err.

Having made my own analysis, I find that the Appellant lacks credibility. Due to multiple contradictions in his testimony and documents, and the irregular manner in which many of the documents were obtained, the Appellant has not established his identity on a balance of probabilities. For all of the foregoing reasons, the Appellant has failed to show that he is XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Senegal.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. The Appellant is not a Convention refugee under section 96 of IRPA or a person in need of protection under section 97 of IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
